function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

security_risk.description:
Security risk levels for actions.

Based on OpenHands security risk levels but adapted for agent-sdk.
Integer values allow for easy comparison and ordering.

summary.description: A concise summary (approximately 10 words) describing what this specific action does. Focus on the key operation and target. Example: 'List all Python files in current directory'

command.description: The shell command to execute. Can be empty string to view additional logs when the previous exit code is `-1`. Can be a special key name when `is_input` is True: `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D/EOF), `C-z` (Ctrl+Z), or any `C-<letter>` for Ctrl sequences; navigation keys `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, `PGDN`; and `TAB`, `ESC`, `BS` (Backspace), `ENTER`. You can only execute one command at a time. Use the platform-appropriate shell syntax described in the tool description when chaining commands.

is_input.description: If True, the command is an input to the running process. If False, the command is executed in the terminal session. Default is False.

timeout.description: Optional. Sets a maximum time limit (in seconds) for running the command. If the command takes longer than this limit, you’ll be asked whether to continue or stop it. If you don’t set a value, the command will instead pause and ask for confirmation when it produces no new output for 30 seconds. Use a higher value if the command is expected to take a long time (like installation or testing), or if it has a known fixed duration (like sleep).

reset.description: If True, reset the terminal by creating a new session. Use this only when the terminal becomes unresponsive. Note that all previously set environment variables and session state will be lost after reset. Cannot be used with is_input=True.

function.name: file_editor
function.description:
Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files in plain-text format
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is an image file (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .bmp), `view` displays the image content
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.


Your current working directory is: /workspace/source
When exploring project structure, start with this directory instead of the root filesystem.

path.description: Absolute path to file or directory.

file_text.description: Required parameter of `create` command, with the content of the file to be created.

insert_line.description: Required parameter of `insert` command. The `new_str` will be inserted AFTER the line `insert_line` of `path`.

Setting `[start_line, -1]` shows all lines from `start_line` to the end of the file.

function.name: think
function.description:
Use the tool to think about something. It will not obtain new information or make any changes to the repository, but just log the thought. Use it when complex reasoning or brainstorming is needed.

Common use cases:
1. When exploring a repository and discovering the source of a bug, call this tool to brainstorm several unique ways of fixing the bug, and assess which change(s) are likely to be simplest and most effective.
2. After receiving test results, use this tool to brainstorm ways to fix failing tests.
3. When planning a complex refactoring, use this tool to outline different approaches and their tradeoffs.
4. When designing a new feature, use this tool to think through architecture decisions and implementation details.
5. When debugging a complex issue, use this tool to organize your thoughts and hypotheses.

The tool simply logs your thought process for better transparency and does not execute any code or make changes.

Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files in plain-text format
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is an image file (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .bmp), `view` displays the image content
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.


Your current working directory is: /workspace/source
When exploring project structure, start with this directory instead of the root filesystem.

path.description: Absolute path to file or directory.

file_text.description: Required parameter of `create` command, with the content of the file to be created.

old_str.description: Required parameter of `str_replace` command containing the string in `path` to replace.

Setting `[start_line, -1]` shows all lines from `start_line` to the end of the file.

function.name: think
function.description:
Use the tool to think about something. It will not obtain new information or make any changes to the repository, but just log the thought. Use it when complex reasoning or brainstorming is needed.

Common use cases:
1. When exploring a repository and discovering the source of a bug, call this tool to brainstorm several unique ways of fixing the bug, and assess which change(s) are likely to be simplest and most effective.
2. After receiving test results, use this tool to brainstorm ways to fix failing tests.
3. When planning a complex refactoring, use this tool to outline different approaches and their tradeoffs.
4. When designing a new feature, use this tool to think through architecture decisions and implementation details.
5. When debugging a complex issue, use this tool to organize your thoughts and hypotheses.

The tool simply logs your thought process for better transparency and does not execute any code or make changes.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

summary.description: A concise summary (approximately 10 words) describing what this specific action does. Focus on the key operation and target. Example: 'List all Python files in current directory'

command.description: The shell command to execute. Can be empty string to view additional logs when the previous exit code is `-1`. Can be a special key name when `is_input` is True: `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D/EOF), `C-z` (Ctrl+Z), or any `C-<letter>` for Ctrl sequences; navigation keys `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, `PGDN`; and `TAB`, `ESC`, `BS` (Backspace), `ENTER`. You can only execute one command at a time. Use the platform-appropriate shell syntax described in the tool description when chaining commands.

is_input.description: If True, the command is an input to the running process. If False, the command is executed in the terminal session. Default is False.

timeout.description: Optional. Sets a maximum time limit (in seconds) for running the command. If the command takes longer than this limit, you’ll be asked whether to continue or stop it. If you don’t set a value, the command will instead pause and ask for confirmation when it produces no new output for 30 seconds. Use a higher value if the command is expected to take a long time (like installation or testing), or if it has a known fixed duration (like sleep).

reset.description: If True, reset the terminal by creating a new session. Use this only when the terminal becomes unresponsive. Note that all previously set environment variables and session state will be lost after reset. Cannot be used with is_input=True.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

  changes, and running processes.

message.content: Now let's try starting docker-compose to test the runtime for erasure requests end-to-end later. First let's design the implementation.

function.arguments:
{"thought":"Let's design the customer data deletion feature.

## Requirements Recap

API:
- POST /v1/customers/:customerId/erasure-requests (auth: privacy:erase scope, Idempotency-Key header 8-200 chars)
  - No body
  - Returns 202 with erasure request: id, customerId, status, attempts, createdAt, updatedAt, completedAt, lastError
  - Idempotency-Key reuse for same customer -> same request returned
  - Idempotency-Key reuse for different customer -> 409
  - If customer already has erasure request, new key returns existing request (don't start a new workflow)
  - 404 if customer doesn't exist or belongs to another merchant (no info leak)
- GET /v1/erasure-requests/:requestId (auth: privacy:erase probably, or read scope? doc says "The API key requires the privacy:erase scope" only mentioned for POST. Let's check doc again.)

Looking at doc: "The API key requires the `privacy:erase` scope." is stated under POST section only. For GET section it doesn't explicitly restate the scope. Let's decide: same scope `privacy:erase` should be required for both, since it's a privacy-sensitive read too. Let's check for consistency - maybe use same scope for both endpoints. I'll use 'privacy:erase' for both endpoints since there's no separate read scope mentioned.

Status lifecycle: pending -> processing -> completed OR failed (failed can retry -> processing -> completed)
lastError: stable error code, no customer data, safe to retry.

Data model:
- New table: customers.erasure_requests
  - id uuid PK
  - merchant_id uuid NOT NULL
  - customer_id uuid NOT NULL (but after completion the customer row itself gets anonymized - retain customer_id? The request's customer_id column can remain since it's just a UUID/foreign key, not personal info. That's fine per retention doc: "minimum information needed to track the request" - customer id (UUID) is not personal info by itself.
  - status text NOT NULL default 'pending' CHECK(status IN ('pending','processing','completed','failed'))
  - attempts integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
  - last_error text
  - created_at, updated_at, completed_at
  - UNIQUE(customer_id) -- only one erasure workflow per customer ever (allows resuming)
  
- Idempotency: Need Idempotency-Key to map determinally to a request, scoped per merchant (since key reuse for different customer should return 409). Let's create a table `customers.erasure_idempotency_keys` (merchant_id, key, customer_id, request_id, created_at) PK(merchant_id key). When creating:
   1. Check if customer exists in customers.customers for the merchant -> else 404
   2. Check existing erasure request for that customer_id (regardless of key) -> if found, and idempotency key not seen before for that particular key+merchant -> just return existing request (per doc: "If the customer already has a data deletion request, a new key returns that existing request instead of starting another workflow.")
   3. Handle idempotency key collision: If key already used by this merchant for a different customer -> 409.
   4. If key already used for this same customer -> return the same request (idempotent).
   
   Essentially: idempotency key is scoped to merchant, mapped to a customer via first use. If key reused with different customer -> conflict do not create/change anything.  If it's used again with same customer, then no-op, just refetch/return current request status (whatever it is, even if pending/completed) since it's a resumed/reposted request.

   Given the additional requirement that "If the customer already has a data deletion request, a new key returns that existing request instead of starting another workflow" -- this means even brand new keys, if a customer already has an existing request, just return the current one (do not create a second workflow, and do not even store the new key?). Actually it might still store the mapping of key->request for that new key, for future POST with same key. Let's just implement it: idempotency keys mapped per (merchant, key) -> customer_id. We check this first: if key exists for merchant:
     - if mapped customer differs from path customerId -> 409
     - else -> look up request for that customer -> return it (200 or 202? Let's check "the same request" - probably return same status as before, likely 202 since it's already accepting semantics). Actually doc example shows 202 on creation. For "Reusing an idempotency key for the same customer returns the same request." It's still same accepted flow, response code 202 presumably (matches saved state). Let's always return 202 on successful resolve (existing or new).  
   If key not yet stored for merchant:
     - Confirm customer exists (else 404, do not store idempotency key)
     - Look for an existing erasure request row for this customer (any key). If found: store new key mapping to same customer + request (for idempotent replay in future), return existing request with 202.
     - Else: create new erasual request row (status pending), enqueue durable job to process it (jobs table, queue 'privacy'), store key mapping, return new request with 202.

This satisfies:
- reuse same key/customer -> same request (via key mapping lookup).
- reuse key with different customer -> 409 (mapped customer differs).
- customer already has an erasure request with a new key -> returns existing request (via existing-request lookup for customer).
- 404 if customer not found for the merchant (only checked when key is new; but if key was already used previously validly, do we still need to check customer existence again? Since customer should still exist (customer row persists though with anonymized data after completion) so this doesn't block.

Also idempotency key uniqueness across merchants isn't an issue since we scope by merchant.

Now, GET /v1/erasure-requests/:requestId: look up request by id scoped by merchant_id; if not found -> 404.

## Async Processing / Worker

Follow the job-lifecycle patterns used elsewhere (operations.jobs, claimJob/completeJob/failJob). Create new queue: 'privacy-erasure' processed by a new worker app 'privacy-worker' (or extend an existing app service, e.g. within customer-service's own background worker, since erasure primarily touches customer-service's own domain data (customers schema) directly, but also payment-service (payments schema - invoices, payment_intents customer_snapshot, refunds.customer_email), notification preferences, documents/manifests, minio objects, search index, mailpit emails, redis cache, analytics_events etc.

This is a cross-service concern - similar to reconciliation-service or document-worker pattern - maybe best implemented as new app: privacy-worker, which claims jobs from 'privacy' queue and performs erasure across all necessary systems directly via the shared database pool (all services share the same Postgres DB per docker-compose, so cross wallet unified DB access is fine, as we saw customer-service repository directly writing to operations.document_manifests etc). Similarly payment-service writes billing_snapshot with customer info; ledger entries have no PII (only reference ids). Provider sandbox has data too. Notifications has destination emails cached in preferences and email deliveries. Search index has customer doc in OpenSearch. Redis cache is a projection in redis with TTL 3600s - so it will expire naturally within an hour; but "must not restore deleted personal data" and "normal processing cannot add it back" - meaning after erasure, Redis cache must not still contain PII. Since Redis key has TTL of 1 hour, but that's still stale PII exposure for up to an hour, violating "already gone from active systems". So the erasure job must explicitly delete this key from Redis too, and this must not get recreated by delayed events reprocessing (idempotent projection worker) - but since customer email/name is anonymized in customers.customers row, if the projection worker re-processes an old CUSTOMER_UPDATED event (unlikely to re-run) it would repopulate PII into redis/opensearch. However inbox_events unique constraint on (consumer, event_id) prevents duplicate. But retries after failures reprocess with same event_id - after 'complete' it's marked 'processed' preventing reprocess. But what about the scenario: customer.created event already processed with original PII in the outbox before deletion; that outbook message already published to Kafka topic and already consumed... it's a done deal, cannot unpublish from Kafka. But the projection into Redis/OpenSearch derived from that already-processed event is what we need to delete via erasure. New events after anonymization (customer.updated with anonymized fields) will overwrite the projection to no longer have PII. Good - this fits pattern used elsewewhere (customer.updated triggers projection update). So as part of erasure workflow, we should emit a customer.updated event (via addOutboxEvent) after anonymizing customer row, causing projection-worker to update Redis and OpenSearch documents with anonymized values. That naturally cleans public projections without needing direct Redis/OpenSearch deletion, PROVIDED projection-worker overwrites with new document (not merge) - looking at project() function it does full "document" object assignment (index call) overwriting the whole doc, then redis.set() overwrites whole key with new JSON. Good, that fully overwrites. 

But timing: our erasure job needs to WAIT for this event to be picked and processed to guarantee "completed only after PII gone from active systems and normal processing cannot add it back" per doc. This could be complex due to async projection lag. Alternative simpler approach: erasure worker also directly deletes/updates Redis key and OpenSearch document synchronously as part of its processing steps (like it directly touches Mailpit and MinIO), rather than relying on eventual projection consistency. This keeps it deterministic and easier to test/complete synchronously. That seems more aligned with how other workflows in this repo directly manipulate storage (e.g., mailpit.ts directly manipulates external system, document worker directly manipulates minio et al). I think it's cleaner to have the erasure job directly issue anonymization queries + direct deletes/updates against Redis, OpenSearch, MinIO objects, Mailpit, in one job execution (steps), each idempotent, and use job attempts/retry to handle partial failures (some external system down) with retries. This matches "workflow must safely resume after a failure or restart... Repeating a request must converge on the same result without duplicating destructive work."

Set customer status maybe 'erased'? Let's check if `status` field has meaning elsewhere (payment service checks customer.status !== 'active' => reject new payments). Setting status = 'erased' would then block new payments after erasure - good side-effect: preventing new payment operations from an erased customer, but doesn't disrupt existing payment history. That seems fine and probably intended: "See a clear outcome... trust deleted." Also this prevents recreating PII via update endpoint since customer is "erased" but PATCH endpoint doesn't check status currently (only version) - could still update email etc. Might be out of scope; but let's keep focus on erasure module itself and not worry about locking further mutations (not explicitly required, but "normal processing cannot add it back" - if merchant PATCH endpoint could set email back to something, that's a different data entry not "adding back deleted data" per se; It's a new value provided by merchant, not restoration. I'll leave existing customer routes unchanged besides erasure.

2. Delete/anonymize addresses (customers.addresses) - which contains PII (kind, line1, line2, city, region, postal_code, country). Simplest: DELETE all addresses for customer (not financial records, no need to retain). 

3. Delete contacts (customers.contacts) - PII, delete all rows for customer.

4. Payment methods refs (customers.payment_method_refs) - contains provider_token, billing_name, billing_address - PII/payment credential info. Need to revoke/anonymize: set status='erased', provider_token = redacted placeholder (cannot keep token since it's sensitive), billing_name=NULL, billing_address=NULL, brand/last4 could stay (last4 arguably still identifies card but maybe permissible to keep for last4 lookup on receipts?) Doc says "Retained records must preserve their financial meaning while no longer identifying the deleted customer." Payment method refs aren't financial records per se (they're payment credentials) - should be deleted/anonymized entirely, not retained, since they aren't required for financial history (payment_intents.customer_snapshot already stores necessary snapshot data for the historical record). Let's redact fully: provider_token -> 'erased', brand/last4/billing_name/billing_address -> NULL, status='erased'.

5. provider_customer_mappings (customers.provider_customer_mappings) - contains provider_customer_id (not exactly PII but linked). Might keep since it's just an ID mapping to provider - not personal data. Leave it; it's just IDs. Actually per data minimization we might delete it since it's no longer needed after erasure (no future operations will occur for an erased customer). But retaining stable ID mapping is harmless (not exposing personal info) - leave as-is, low risk. I'll leave it alone; not personal data.

This is customer-generated content potentially containing PII. Should we delete these support messages? The task didn't explicitly mention support tickets in retention doc, but the broad statement "removes a customer's personal data from every PayFlow-controlled system that actively stores, processes, or exposes it" implies erasing support content too, since it's not required for financial retention. Let's redact body/subject to placeholder and detach author reference (set body/subject to redacted marker, keep ticket for shared participants? Since a ticket might have multiple participants (shared record used by other customers) - "Do not alter data belonging to other customers." Since support_tickets/messages are per single customer with ticket_id unique to that ticket (participants table associates multiple customers with same ticket though - a "shared ticket" scenario). Let's check "docs/privacy-and-retention.md" wording again: "removes a customer's personal data from every PayFlow-controlled system that actively stores, processes, or exposes it." -> support ticket messages (body written by customer) could contain PII entered by customer, and ticket subject too. Actually let's check indices/relationships: support_participants links ticket_id to customer_id (potentially multiple customers per ticket if that feature existed, but current API only adds the creating customer). function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

function.description:
Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files in plain-text format
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is an image file (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .bmp), `view` displays the image content
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.

function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

function.name: file_editor
function.description:
Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files in plain-text format
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is an image file (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .bmp), `view` displays the image content
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.

terminal
function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

summary.description: A concise summary (approximately 10 words) describing what this specific action does. Focus on the key operation and target. Example: 'List all Python files in current directory'

command.description: The shell command to execute. Can be empty string to view additional logs when the previous exit code is `-1`. Can be a special key name when `is_input` is True: `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D/EOF), `C-z` (Ctrl+Z), or any `C-<letter>` for Ctrl sequences; navigation keys `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, `PGDN`; and `TAB`, `ESC`, `BS` (Backspace), `ENTER`. You can only execute one command at a time. Use the platform-appropriate shell syntax described in the tool description when chaining commands.

is_input.description: If True, the command is an input to the running process. If False, the command is executed in the terminal session. Default is False.

timeout.description: Optional. Sets a maximum time limit (in seconds) for running the command. If the command takes longer than this limit, you’ll be asked whether to continue or stop it. If you don’t set a value, the command will instead pause and ask for confirmation when it produces no new output for 30 seconds. Use a higher value if the command is expected to take a long time (like installation or testing), or if it has a known fixed duration (like sleep).

reset.description: If True, reset the terminal by creating a new session. Use this only when the terminal becomes unresponsive. Note that all previously set environment variables and session state will be lost after reset. Cannot be used with is_input=True.

function.name: file_editor
function.description:
Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files in plain-text format
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is an image file (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .bmp), `view` displays the image content
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.


Your current working directory is: /workspace/source
When exploring project structure, start with this directory instead of the root filesystem.

* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.

  changes, and running processes.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs

* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

Use the tool to think about something. It will not obtain new information or make any changes to the repository, but just log the thought. Use it when complex reasoning or brainstorming is needed.

Common use cases:
1. When exploring a repository and discovering the source of a bug, call this tool to brainstorm several unique ways of fixing the bug, and assess which change(s) are likely to be simplest and most effective.
2. After receiving test results, use this tool to brainstorm ways to fix failing tests.
3. When planning a complex refactoring, use this tool to outline different approaches and their tradeoffs.
4. When designing a new feature, use this tool to think through architecture decisions and implementation details.
5. When debugging a complex issue, use this tool to organize your thoughts and hypotheses.

The tool simply logs your thought process for better transparency and does not execute any code or make changes.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

summary.description: A concise summary (approximately 10 words) describing what this specific action does. Focus on the key operation and target. Example: 'List all Python files in current directory'

command.description: The shell command to execute. Can be empty string to view additional logs when the previous exit code is `-1`. Can be a special key name when `is_input` is True: `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D/EOF), `C-z` (Ctrl+Z), or any `C-<letter>` for Ctrl sequences; navigation keys `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, `PGDN`; and `TAB`, `ESC`, `BS` (Backspace), `ENTER`. You can only execute one command at a time. Use the platform-appropriate shell syntax described in the tool description when chaining commands.

is_input.description: If True, the command is an input to the running process. If False, the command is executed in the terminal session. Default is False.

timeout.description: Optional. Sets a maximum time limit (in seconds) for running the command. If the command takes longer than this limit, you’ll be asked whether to continue or stop it. If you don’t set a value, the command will instead pause and ask for confirmation when it produces no new output for 30 seconds. Use a higher value if the command is expected to take a long time (like installation or testing), or if it has a known fixed duration (like sleep).

reset.description: If True, reset the terminal by creating a new session. Use this only when the terminal becomes unresponsive. Note that all previously set environment variables and session state will be lost after reset. Cannot be used with is_input=True.

function.name: file_editor
function.description:
Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files in plain-text format
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is an image file (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .bmp), `view` displays the image content
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.


Your current working directory is: /workspace/source
When exploring project structure, start with this directory instead of the root filesystem.

  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:

* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.

* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

Security risk levels for actions.

Based on OpenHands security risk levels but adapted for agent-sdk.
Integer values allow for easy comparison and ordering.

summary.description: A concise summary (approximately 10 words) describing what this specific action does. Focus on the key operation and target. Example: 'List all Python files in current directory'

command.description: The shell command to execute. Can be empty string to view additional logs when the previous exit code is `-1`. Can be a special key name when `is_input` is True: `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D/EOF), `C-z` (Ctrl+Z), or any `C-<letter>` for Ctrl sequences; navigation keys `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, `PGDN`; and `TAB`, `ESC`, `BS` (Backspace), `ENTER`. You can only execute one command at a time. Use the platform-appropriate shell syntax described in the tool description when chaining commands.

is_input.description: If True, the command is an input to the running process. If False, the command is executed in the terminal session. Default is False.

timeout.description: Optional. Sets a maximum time limit (in seconds) for running the command. If the command takes longer than this limit, you’ll be asked whether to continue or stop it. If you don’t set a value, the command will instead pause and ask for confirmation when it produces no new output for 30 seconds. Use a higher value if the command is expected to take a long time (like installation or testing), or if it has a known fixed duration (like sleep).

reset.description: If True, reset the terminal by creating a new session. Use this only when the terminal becomes unresponsive. Note that all previously set environment variables and session state will be lost after reset. Cannot be used with is_input=True.

function.name: file_editor
function.description:
Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files in plain-text format
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is an image file (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .bmp), `view` displays the image content
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.


Your current working directory is: /workspace/source
When exploring project structure, start with this directory instead of the root filesystem.

Setting `[start_line, -1]` shows all lines from `start_line` to the end of the file.

Common use cases:
1. When exploring a repository and discovering the source of a bug, call this tool to brainstorm several unique ways of fixing the bug, and assess which change(s) are likely to be simplest and most effective.
2. After receiving test results, use this tool to brainstorm ways to fix failing tests.
3. When planning a complex refactoring, use this tool to outline different approaches and their tradeoffs.
4. When designing a new feature, use this tool to think through architecture decisions and implementation details.
5. When debugging a complex issue, use this tool to organize your thoughts and hypotheses.

The tool simply logs your thought process for better transparency and does not execute any code or make changes.

Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files in plain-text format
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is an image file (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .bmp), `view` displays the image content
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.

When exploring project structure, start with this directory instead of the root filesystem.

The tool simply logs your thought process for better transparency and does not execute any code or make changes.

function.name: terminal
terminal
function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

command.description: The shell command to execute. Can be empty string to view additional logs when the previous exit code is `-1`. Can be a special key name when `is_input` is True: `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D/EOF), `C-z` (Ctrl+Z), or any `C-<letter>` for Ctrl sequences; navigation keys `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, `PGDN`; and `TAB`, `ESC`, `BS` (Backspace), `ENTER`. You can only execute one command at a time. Use the platform-appropriate shell syntax described in the tool description when chaining commands.

is_input.description: If True, the command is an input to the running process. If False, the command is executed in the terminal session. Default is False.

timeout.description: Optional. Sets a maximum time limit (in seconds) for running the command. If the command takes longer than this limit, you’ll be asked whether to continue or stop it. If you don’t set a value, the command will instead pause and ask for confirmation when it produces no new output for 30 seconds. Use a higher value if the command is expected to take a long time (like installation or testing), or if it has a known fixed duration (like sleep).

reset.description: If True, reset the terminal by creating a new session. Use this only when the terminal becomes unresponsive. Note that all previously set environment variables and session state will be lost after reset. Cannot be used with is_input=True.

function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.

message.content: Let's create an AGENTS.md with useful repository insights for future sessions.

function.arguments:
{"command":"create","path":"/workspace/source/AGENTS.md","file_text":"# Repository notes for agents

PayFlow is a small multi-service TypeScript monorepo (Fastify HTTP services +
background workers) sharing one Postgres database across bounded contexts
(`customers`, `payments`, `operations`, `platform`, `provider_sandbox`
schemas). Services talk to Postgres directly (no ORM), publish domain events
through a transactional outbox (`operations.outbox_events`) onto Kafka
(Redpanda), and use Redis/OpenSearch/MinIO/Mailpit as read/side-effect stores.

## Environment
- No git repo is present in `/workspace/source` (this is a snapshot, not a
  git checkout) — don't expect `git log`/`git status` to work.
- Node 22, npm workspoces-free single `package.json`. `npm ci` then
  `npm run typecheck` / `npm run lint` / `npm test` are fast (no docker
  needed) and should be run after any change.
- Full integration testing requires `docker compose up -d`. The `mailpit`
  container's healthcheck must run `wget -Y off ...` (not plain `wget`)
  because this sandbox injects an `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` env var into
  every container, which busybox `wget` honors even for `localhost` unless
  proxying is explicitly disabled with `-Y off`.
- `docker compose --profile tools run --rm seed|runtime-check` and
  `npm run scenario` / `npm run smoke` are the existing end-to-end checks;
  `scripts/check-runtime.ts` asserts the whole system (outbox, jobs, emails,
  ledger, receipts, Redis/OpenSearch/MinIO/Mailpit parity) converged.

## Background workers
Every worker in `apps/*-worker` follows the same shape: a `claim*`/`complete*`/
`fail*` lifecycle module (see `packages/operations/src/job-lifecycle.ts`,
`packages/notifications/src/delivery-lifecycle.ts`) backed by a Postgres row
with `status`, `attempts`, `available_at`/`lease_expires_at`, polled in a
`while (!signal.aborted)` loop with `SKIP LOCKED`, plus a periodic
"recover expired leases" sweep. Failures always store a short, stable string
in `last_error` (never a raw error message that could leak customer data).

## Customer data erasure (privacy)
Implements `docs/privacy-api.md` / `docs/privacy-and-retention.md`.
- `customers.erasure_requests` (one row per customer per merchant, unique on
  `(merchant_id, customer_id)`) is both the API-visible request record *and*
  the durable work queue for `apps/privacy-worker`.
- `customers.erasure_idempotency_keys` scopes `Idempotency-Key` reuse to the
  merchant and maps it to the customer it was first used for
  (`apps/customer-service/src/erasure-service.ts` implements the exact
  replay/conflict/reuse rules from `docs/privacy-api.md`).
- All erasure side effects live in `packages/privacy/src/erasure-workflow.ts`
  (`eraseCustomerData`) and are idempotent: re-running it (after a retry or a
  worker restart) always converges on the same fully-redacted state. Steps:
  purge captured Mailpit messages, rewrite stored receipt/invoice JSON in
  MinIO in place (redacting the embedded `customer` object, keeping
  amounts/lines), anonymize `customers.customers` (+ addresses/contacts/
  payment methods/support content), anonymize `customer_snapshot` /
  `billing_snapshot` on existing `payments.payment_intents` /
  `payments.invoices` (financial fields untouched), redact `refunds.
  customer_email`, then clear the Redis/OpenSearch customer projections
  (which get lazily repopulated in redacted form by the normal
  `customer.updated` event the workflow emits, exercised by
  `apps/projection-worker`).
- Failures are mapped to a small closed set of PII-free codes in
  `packages/privacy/src/errors.ts` (`ErasureStepError`/`toErasureErrorCode`)
  so `lastError` returned by `GET /v1/erasure-requests/:id` never contains
  customer data.
- An erased customer's `status` becomes `'erased'`, which the existing
  `payment-service` "customer is not active" check already blocks new
  payments against — no extra guard was needed there.
"}

function.arguments:
{"message":"Implemented customer data deletion (erasure) for PayFlow per `docs/privacy-api.md` and `docs/privacy-and-retention.md`.

## What was built

**API (via api-gateway → customer-service)**
- `POST /v1/customers/:customerId/erasure-requests` — requires `privacy:erase` scope + `Idempotency-Key` header (8–200 chars). Returns `202` with the erasure request. Idempotency is scoped per-merchant: reusing a key for the same customer replays the same request; reusing it for a different customer returns `409`; a brand-new key for a customer that already has a request returns that existing request instead of starting a second workflow. Returns `404` (no data leak) if the customer doesn't exist or belongs to another merchant.
- `GET /v1/erasure-requests/:requestId` — requires `privacy:erase` scope. Returns `404` if the request doesn't exist or belongs to another merchant. Statuses: `pending` → `processing` → `completed`/`failed` (failed is safely retryable), with a small closed set of PII-free `lastError` codes.

**Async processing**
- New `apps/privacy-worker` service polls `customers.erasure_requests` (new table, also used as the durable queue) with the same claim/lease/retry pattern used by the other workers in this repo (`SKIP LOCKED`, bounded exponential backoff, lease-expiry recovery).
- `packages/privacy/src/erasure-workflow.ts` (`eraseCustomerData`) performs all erasure steps idempotently: purges captured Mailpit emails, rewrites stored receipt/invoice JSON in MinIO in place (redacting the embedded customer profile, preserving amounts/lines/currency), anonymizes `customers.customers` + addresses/contacts/payment methods/support tickets & messages, anonymizes `customer_snapshot`/`billing_snapshot` on existing payments/invoices, redacts `refunds.customer_email`, clears Redis/OpenSearch customer projections, and emits a redacted `customer.updated` event (which the existing projection worker uses to repopulate Redis/OpenSearch with the anonymized data) plus a `customer.erasure.completed` event.
- New migration `009_customer_erasure.sql` adds `customers.erasure_requests` and `customers.erasure_idempotency_keys`.

**Financial/retention correctness**
- Payments, invoices, refunds, ledger entries, and captures are all preserved and remain financially correct (amounts/currency/totals untouched); only PII fields are redacted.
- An erased customer's `status` becomes `erased`, which the existing payment-service "customer is not active" check already blocks new payments against — verified end-to-end that new payments are rejected while existing-payment refunds still succeed (and use the already-redacted snapshot, so no new PII leaks).
- Other customers/merchants are untouched (verified addresses/contacts/support tickets for other customers survive; cross-tenant erasure/status lookups are blocked with 404).

## Verification performed
- `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`, `npm test` (added `tests/privacy.test.ts`) all pass.
- Full `docker compose up` + `seed` + `scenario` + `smoke` + `runtime-check` pass both before and after exercising erasure requests.
- Manually exercised: missing idempotency key (400), create (202), replay same key/customer, replay same key/different customer (409), new key on already-requested customer, nonexistent customer (404), cross-tenant customer (404), GET status, GET nonexistent (404), GET cross-tenant (404), and end-to-end completion — inspecting Postgres, Redis, OpenSearch, MinIO, and Mailpit directly to confirm PII was gone and financial data intact.
- Exercised the failure/retry path by stopping Mailpit mid-request: the request correctly went to `failed` with a stable `mail_provider_unavailable` code, then completed automatically once Mailpit came back, with no duplicated/partial side effects.

## Incidental fix
- The `mailpit` healthcheck used plain `wget`, which respects this sandbox's injected `HTTP_PROXY` even for `localhost`, so `docker compose up` never became healthy. Fixed by adding `-Y off` to disable proxying for that health check only (unrelated to the feature itself, but needed to run docker compose in this environment).

Also added `AGENTS.md` with repository/architecture notes for future sessions.

No git repository exists in this workspace, so no commit/PR was created — all changes are on disk in `/workspace/source`."}

function.description:
Execute a shell command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one shell command at a time.
  If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;`.
* Persistent session: Environment variables, virtual environments, and
  working directory changes persist across commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands pause for confirmation after 10 seconds without
  new output unless you provide a longer `timeout`.
* Shell options: Do NOT use `set -e`, `set -eu`, or `set -euo pipefail`.
  The runtime may not support them reliably.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and
  redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For long-running commands, set the `timeout` parameter accordingly.
* If a command returns exit code `-1`, it hit the soft timeout and is
  still running. With `is_input=true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c`, `C-d`, or `C-z`
  - Send navigation keys like `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `TAB`,
    `ESC`, `BS`, `HOME`, `END`, `PGUP`, and `PGDN`
  - Send any `C-<letter>` Ctrl sequence such as `C-a`, `C-e`, or `C-l`

### Best Practices
* Verify a parent directory exists before creating files or directories.
* Prefer absolute paths and avoid excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Large output may be truncated before being returned.

### Terminal Reset
* Set `reset=true` to create a fresh terminal session if the current one
  becomes unresponsive.
* Resetting the terminal clears environment variables, working directory
  changes, and running processes.
